claim: Plexin-B2 is expressed in proliferating CGN precursors in the outer external granule layer (oEGL) of the cerebellum.
source: Although in the cerebellum Plexin-B2 is only expressed by proliferating CGN precursors in the outer external granule layer (oEGL), its function in CGN development is still elusive.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1A-C and by in situ hybridization data in Figure 1F showing Plexin-B2 expression restricted to the oEGL.

claim: Plexin-B2 expression is downregulated in post-mitotic CGNs.
source: Strikingly, Plexin-B2 is only expressed in the oEGL and downregulated in post-mitotic CGNs (Friedel et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Friedel et al., 2007 and by immunostaining data in Figure 1B showing Plexin-B2 is absent in Tag1+ postmitotic CGNs.

claim: Plexin-B2 deletion leads to aberrant lamination of cerebellar granule neurons and Purkinje cells.
source: Plexin-B2 deletion leads to aberrant lamination of cerebellar granule neurons (CGNs) and Purkinje cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figures 1D, 1G, 1H, 2A, and 3 showing disorganized cerebellar cortex layers in Plxnb2 mutants.

claim: Proliferating CGNs in Plxnb2 mutants escape the oEGL and mix with newborn postmitotic CGNs.
source: We show that proliferating CGNs in Plxnb2 mutants not only escape the oEGL and mix with newborn postmitotic CGNs.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data in Figure 4A-B showing EdU+ and Ki67+ proliferating cells intermingled with Tag1+ postmitotic CGNs in the EGL of mutants.

claim: Motility of mitotic precursors and early postmitotic CGNs is altered in Plxnb2 mutants.
source: Furthermore, motility of mitotic precursors and early postmitotic CGNs is altered.
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data in Figures 8 and 10 showing altered migration patterns and increased motility of multipolar CGNs in mutant explants.

claim: Plxnb2 deletion leads to the formation of ectopic patches of CGNs at the cerebellar surface.
source: Together, this leads to the formation of ectopic patches of CGNs at the cerebellar surface and an intermingling of normally time-stamped parallel fibers in the molecular layer (ML), and aberrant arborization of Purkinje cell dendrites.
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data in Figures 1D, 1H, 3B, 3D, and 5H showing ectopic CGN accumulations at the cerebellar surface in mutants.

claim: Plxnb2 deletion leads to intermingling of normally time-stamped parallel fibers in the molecular layer.
source: Together, this leads to the formation of ectopic patches of CGNs at the cerebellar surface and an intermingling of normally time-stamped parallel fibers in the molecular layer (ML), and aberrant arborization of Purkinje cell dendrites.
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Figure 6A showing overlap of early-born (GFP+) and late-born (tdTomato+) parallel fibers in the ML of mutants.

claim: Plxnb2 deletion leads to aberrant arborization of Purkinje cell dendrites.
source: Together, this leads to the formation of ectopic patches of CGNs at the cerebellar surface and an intermingling of normally time-stamped parallel fibers in the molecular layer (ML), and aberrant arborization of Purkinje cell dendrites.
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data in Figures 1G, 1H, 6B, and 6—figure supplement 1A showing disorganized Purkinje cell dendrites in mutants.

claim: Plexin-B2 restricts CGN motility.
source: There results suggest that Plexin-B2 restricts CGN motility and might have a function in cytokinesis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from time-lapse data in Figures 8 and 10 showing increased motility and altered migration patterns in Plxnb2 mutant CGNs.

claim: Plexin-B2 might have a function in cytokinesis.
source: There results suggest that Plexin-B2 restricts CGN motility and might have a function in cytokinesis.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on observations in Figure 4D showing increased EdU+/H3P+ cells and Figure 10E showing delayed transition to bipolar morphology after cytokinesis in mutants.

claim: Plexins are single-pass transmembrane receptors for Semaphorins.
source: Plexins are single-pass transmembrane receptors for Semaphorins regulating cell-cell interactions in normal and pathological contexts (Pasterkamp, 2012; Tamagnone et al., 1999; Worzfeld and Offermanns, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Semaphorin/Plexin signaling has been involved in axon guidance and regeneration in the developing CNS.
source: In the developing central nervous system (CNS), Semaphorin/Plexin signaling has been involved in axon guidance and regeneration, neuronal migration (Pasterkamp, 2012; Sekine et al., 2019; Yoshida, 2012), and synaptogenesis (Hung et al., 2010; Kuzirian et al., 2013; Molofsky et al., 2014; Orr et al., 2017; Pecho-Vrieseling et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Semaphorin/Plexin signaling has been involved in neuronal migration in the developing CNS.
source: In the developing central nervous system (CNS), Semaphorin/Plexin signaling has been involved in axon guidance and regeneration, neuronal migration (Pasterkamp, 2012; Sekine et al., 2019; Yoshida, 2012), and synaptogenesis (Hung et al., 2010; Kuzirian et al., 2013; Molofsky et al., 2014; Orr et al., 2017; Pecho-Vrieseling et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Semaphorin/Plexin signaling has been involved in synaptogenesis in the developing CNS.
source: In the developing central nervous system (CNS), Semaphorin/Plexin signaling has been involved in axon guidance and regeneration, neuronal migration (Pasterkamp, 2012; Sekine et al., 2019; Yoshida, 2012), and synaptogenesis (Hung et al., 2010; Kuzirian et al., 2013; Molofsky et al., 2014; Orr et al., 2017; Pecho-Vrieseling et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Plexins are linked to autism spectrum disorders, multiple sclerosis, Alzheimer's, pathological pain, and spinal cord injury.
source: There is also evidence linking plexins to a variety of neurological diseases such as autism spectrum disorders, multiple sclerosis, Alzheimer's, pathological pain, and spinal cord injury (Van Battum et al., 2015; Binamé et al., 2019; Paldy et al., 2017; Zhou et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: B-type plexins form a small subclass of plexins with three members (Plexin-B1, -B2, and -B3) in mammals.
source: B-type plexins form a small subclass of plexins, with three members (Plexin-B1, -B2, and -B3) in mammals (Pasterkamp, 2012; Worzfeld et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: B-type plexins are expressed by neurons, astrocytes, and oligodendrocytes.
source: B-type plexins are not only expressed by neurons but also astrocytes and oligodendrocytes, with some overlapping expression.
evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge about plexin expression patterns.

claim: The cytoplasmic domain of plexins contains a GTPase activating protein (GAP) with an embedded Rho-binding domain (RBD).
source: Like all plexins, their cytoplasmic domain contains a GTPase activating protein (GAP) in which a Rho-binding domain (RBD) is embedded (Oinuma et al., 2004; Seiradake et al., 2016; Tong et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to structural biology literature.

claim: The C-terminal region of B-type plexins interacts with PDZ domains of PDZeRhoGEF and LARG.
source: Their C-terminal region also interacts with the PDZ (PSD-95, Dlg-1 and ZO-1) domains of two guanine nucleotide exchange factors (GEF), PDZeRhoGEF and leukemia-associated RhoGEF (LARG) (Pascoe et al., 2015; Perrot et al., 2002; Seiradake et al., 2016; Swiercz et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Plexin dimerization is induced by Semaphorin binding and activates GAP activity.
source: Plexin dimerization is induced by Semaphorin binding and activates GAP activity, but dimerization was reported to be weaker for Plexin-B2 which might primarily act as a monomer (Wang et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to structural and biochemical studies.

claim: Plexin-B2 dimerization is weaker than other plexins and it might primarily act as a monomer.
source: Plexin dimerization is induced by Semaphorin binding and activates GAP activity, but dimerization was reported to be weaker for Plexin-B2 which might primarily act as a monomer (Wang et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Wang et al., 2012 and Zhang et al., 2015.

claim: Class four transmembrane semaphorins are the main ligands for B-type plexins.
source: Class four transmembrane semaphorins are the main ligands for B-type plexins (Pasterkamp, 2012; Seiradake et al., 2016; Tamagnone et al., 1999) but Plexin-B1 and Plexin-B2 were also shown to interact with the receptor tyrosine kinases ErbB-2 and MET (Giordano et al., 2002; Swiercz et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Plexin-B1 and Plexin-B2 interact with the receptor tyrosine kinases ErbB-2 and MET.
source: Class four transmembrane semaphorins are the main ligands for B-type plexins (Pasterkamp, 2012; Seiradake et al., 2016; Tamagnone et al., 1999) but Plexin-B1 and Plexin-B2 were also shown to interact with the receptor tyrosine kinases ErbB-2 and MET (Giordano et al., 2002; Swiercz et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Giordano et al., 2002 and Swiercz et al., 2004.

claim: Plexin-B2 is a receptor for angiogenin.
source: It was also recently demonstrated that Plexin-B2 is a receptor for angiogenin, a secreted ribonuclease involved in angiogenesis and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (Subramanian et al., 2008; Yu et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Subramanian et al., 2008 and Yu et al., 2017.

claim: Knockout mice for all B-type plexins have been generated.
source: Knockout mice for all B-type plexins have been generated but surprisingly, no major brain anomalies have been detected so far in Plxnb1 (Deng et al., 2007) and Plxnb3 (Worzfeld et al., 2009) knockouts.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature describing knockout mouse models.

claim: No major brain anomalies have been detected in Plxnb1 and Plxnb3 knockout mice.
source: Knockout mice for all B-type plexins have been generated but surprisingly, no major brain anomalies have been detected so far in Plxnb1 (Deng et al., 2007) and Plxnb3 (Worzfeld et al., 2009) knockouts.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Deng et al., 2007 and Worzfeld et al., 2009.

claim: Plxnb1 knockout mice show altered photoreceptor outer segment phagocytosis in the retina.
source: However, altered photoreceptor outer segment phagocytosis in the retina (Bulloj et al., 2018) and abnormal migration of Gonadotropin hormone releasing hormone neurons to the hypothalamus (Giacobini et al., 2008) were reported in Plxnb1 knockouts.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Bulloj et al., 2018.

claim: Plxnb1 knockout mice show abnormal migration of Gonadotropin hormone releasing hormone neurons to the hypothalamus.
source: However, altered photoreceptor outer segment phagocytosis in the retina (Bulloj et al., 2018) and abnormal migration of Gonadotropin hormone releasing hormone neurons to the hypothalamus (Giacobini et al., 2008) were reported in Plxnb1 knockouts.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Giacobini et al., 2008.

claim: Plxnb2 knockout mice display severe CNS defects including exencephaly and increased apoptosis.
source: In contrast, Plxnb2 knockout mice display severe CNS defects including exencephaly and increased apoptosis (Deng et al., 2007; Friedel et al., 2007), nociceptive hypersensitivity (Paldy et al., 2017), and fear response (Simonetti et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Deng et al., 2007 and Friedel et al., 2007.

claim: Plxnb2 knockout mice display nociceptive hypersensitivity.
source: In contrast, Plxnb2 knockout mice display severe CNS defects including exencephaly and increased apoptosis (Deng et al., 2007; Friedel et al., 2007), nociceptive hypersensitivity (Paldy et al., 2017), and fear response (Simonetti et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Paldy et al., 2017.

claim: Plxnb2 knockout mice display altered fear response.
source: In contrast, Plxnb2 knockout mice display severe CNS defects including exencephaly and increased apoptosis (Deng et al., 2007; Friedel et al., 2007), nociceptive hypersensitivity (Paldy et al., 2017), and fear response (Simonetti et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Simonetti et al., 2021.

claim: The most striking neurodevelopmental defect in Plxnb2 knockout mice is severe disorganization of the layering and foliation of the cerebellar cortex.
source: The most striking neurodevelopmental defect reported in Plxnb2 knockout mice is a severe disorganization of the layering and foliation of the cerebellar cortex (Deng et al., 2007; Friedel et al., 2007; Maier et al., 2011; Worzfeld et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple published studies and by data in Figures 1D, 1H, 2, and 3.

claim: The cerebellum contains about 9 neuronal types.
source: The cerebellum contains a limited and well-characterized number of neuronal types (about 9) and its cortex has only three layers: the inner granular layer (IGL), the deepest one, contains granule cells (CGNs), the Purkinje cell layer, and most externally, the molecular layer, which hosts Purkinje cell dendrites, CGN axons and two types of interneurons, the stellate and basket cells (Sotelo, 2011; Voogd, 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Sotelo, 2011 and Voogd, 2003.

claim: The cerebellar cortex has three layers: the inner granular layer (IGL), the Purkinje cell layer, and the molecular layer.
source: The cerebellum contains a limited and well-characterized number of neuronal types (about 9) and its cortex has only three layers: the inner granular layer (IGL), the deepest one, contains granule cells (CGNs), the Purkinje cell layer, and most externally, the molecular layer, which hosts Purkinje cell dendrites, CGN axons and two types of interneurons, the stellate and basket cells (Sotelo, 2011; Voogd, 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to established cerebellar anatomy literature.

claim: Purkinje cell axons are the sole output of the cerebellar cortex.
source: Purkinje cell axons are the sole output of the cerebellar cortex.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of cerebellar anatomy.

claim: Cerebellar neurons originate from the ventricular zone of the cerebellum primordium, except CGNs and unipolar brush cells that arise in the upper rhombic lip.
source: Cerebellar neurons originate from the ventricular zone of the cerebellum primordium, except CGNs and unipolar brush cells that arise in the so-called upper rhombic lip (Leto et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Leto et al., 2016.

claim: In the mouse brain, cerebellar CGNs account for about half of all neurons.
source: In the mouse brain, cerebellar CGNs account for about half of the neurons all generated after birth from progenitors localized in a transient neuroepithelium, the external granular layer (EGL), occupying the surface of the cerebellum until about the third postnatal week (Chédotal, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Chédotal, 2010.

claim: CGNs are generated after birth from progenitors in the external granular layer (EGL).
source: In the mouse brain, cerebellar CGNs account for about half of the neurons all generated after birth from progenitors localized in a transient neuroepithelium, the external granular layer (EGL), occupying the surface of the cerebellum until about the third postnatal week (Chédotal, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Chédotal, 2010 and is established knowledge.

claim: The EGL occupies the surface of the cerebellum until about the third postnatal week.
source: In the mouse brain, cerebellar CGNs account for about half of the neurons all generated after birth from progenitors localized in a transient neuroepithelium, the external granular layer (EGL), occupying the surface of the cerebellum until about the third postnatal week (Chédotal, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Chédotal, 2010 and by data in Figure 1C showing EGL regression.

claim: The EGL develops embryonically as CGN precursors migrate from the rhombic lip to colonize the surface of the cerebellar anlage.
source: The EGL develops embryonically as CGN precursors migrate from the rhombic lip to colonize the surface of the cerebellar anlage (Miale and Sidman, 1961).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Miale and Sidman, 1961.

claim: Symmetrical division amplifies the pool of CGN precursors until birth.
source: Symmetrical division amplifies the pool of precursors until birth, after which they start dividing asymmetrically to generate CGNs.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of CGN development.

claim: After birth, CGN precursors start dividing asymmetrically to generate CGNs.
source: Symmetrical division amplifies the pool of precursors until birth, after which they start dividing asymmetrically to generate CGNs.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of CGN development.

claim: Post-mitotic CGNs segregate from dividing precursors and move inward splitting the EGL into two sublayers: the outer EGL (oEGL) containing proliferating cells and the inner EGL (iEGL) containing newly born CGNs.
source: Post-mitotic CGNs segregate from dividing precursors and move inward splitting the EGL into two sublayers: the outer EGL (oEGL) containing proliferating cells and the inner EGL (iEGL) containing newly born CGNs.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of EGL organization and is illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: In the iEGL, CGNs migrate tangentially, grow two processes (their presumptive axons or parallel fibers) and adopt a bipolar morphology.
source: In the iEGL, CGNs migrate tangentially (parallel to the cerebellar surface), grow two processes (their presumptive axons or parallel fibers) and adopt a bipolar morphology (Komuro et al., 2001; Cajal, 1909).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Komuro et al., 2001 and Cajal, 1909, and is illustrated in Figure 5B.

claim: CGNs extend a third process perpendicular to the surface, which attaches to Bergmann glia fibers and guides the inward radial migration of CGNs across the molecular layer to the inner granule cell layer.
source: CGNs next extend a third process perpendicular to the surface, which attaches to Bergmann glia fibers and guide the inward radial migration of CGNs across the molecular layer to the inner granule cell layer.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of CGN radial migration and is illustrated in Figure 5B.

claim: The lack of Plexin-B2 maintains some migrating CGNs in a proliferating state which leads to a massive disorganization of cerebellar cortex layers.
source: The phenotypic analysis of two Plxnb2 complete knockout lines showed that the lack of Plexin-B2 maintains some migrating CGNs in a proliferating state which leads to a massive disorganization of cerebellar cortex layers (Deng et al., 2007; Friedel et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Deng et al., 2007 and Friedel et al., 2007, and by data in Figures 4 and 5 showing proliferating bipolar CGNs in mutants.

claim: This phenotype has been observed in a conditional knockout lacking Plexin-B2 in CGN precursors.
source: This phenotype has been also observed in a conditional knockout lacking Plexin-B2 in CGN precursors (Worzfeld et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Worzfeld et al., 2014.

claim: The exact consequences of Plexin-B2 deficiency on CGN development are unknown and were not studied at a cellular level.
source: However, the exact consequences of Plexin-B2 deficiency on CGN development are unknown and were not studied at a cellular level.
evidence: The claim is an assessment of the state of knowledge prior to this study.

claim: The transition from a multipolar to a bipolar morphology is altered in absence of Plexin-B2.
source: We show that the transition from a multipolar to a bipolar morphology, the migration speed and CGN axon distribution are altered in absence of Plexin-B2.
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Figures 7E and 10—figure supplement 1B showing increased proportion of multipolar cells in mutant explants.

claim: The migration speed of CGNs is altered in absence of Plexin-B2.
source: We show that the transition from a multipolar to a bipolar morphology, the migration speed and CGN axon distribution are altered in absence of Plexin-B2.
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Figure 8C showing altered migration patterns with increased reverse movement in mutant CGNs.

claim: CGN axon distribution is altered in absence of Plexin-B2.
source: We show that the transition from a multipolar to a bipolar morphology, the migration speed and CGN axon distribution are altered in absence of Plexin-B2.
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Figures 5H and 6A showing disorganized parallel fiber distribution in the molecular layer of mutants.

claim: Proliferating CGN precursors in the EGL can be labeled using 5-Ethynyl-2'-deoxyuridine (EdU).
source: In the mouse cerebellum, which matures during the first three postnatal weeks, proliferating CGN precursors in the EGL, which can be labeled using 5-Ethynyl-2'-deoxyuridine (EdU), express Plexin-B2 (Friedel et al., 2007; Worzfeld et al., 2004; Figure 1A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B showing EdU labeling of proliferating cells in the oEGL.

claim: Plexin-B2 expression diminishes when CGNs start to migrate in a tangential direction.
source: Plexin-B2 expression diminishes when CGNs start to migrate in a tangential direction (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data in Figure 1B showing Plexin-B2 is absent in Tag1+ tangentially migrating CGNs.

claim: As the EGL resorbs and becomes depleted of CGN precursors and post-mitotic CGNs, Plexin-B2 expression progressively disappears.
source: As the EGL resorbs (Figure 1C) and becomes depleted of CGN precursors and post-mitotic CGNs, Plexin-B2 expression progressively disappears (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Figure 1C showing progressive loss of Plexin-B2 expression as the EGL regresses from P6 to P15.

claim: A small fraction of Plxnb2-/- mutant mice, bred in the CD1 background, survive and display severe cerebellar disorganization.
source: As previously shown, a small fraction of Plxnb2-/- mutant mice, bred in the CD1 background, survive and display severe cerebellar disorganization (Friedel et al., 2007; Maier et al., 2011; Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Friedel et al., 2007 and Maier et al., 2011, and by data in Figure 1D showing disorganized cerebellum in Plxnb2-/- mice.

claim: En1Cre;Plxnb2fl/fl and Wnt1-Cre;Plxnb2fl/fl lines were viable.
source: Both En1Cre;Plxnb2fl/fl and Wnt1-Cre;Plxnb2fl/fl lines were viable.
evidence: The claim is an observation from the generation of conditional knockout mice.

claim: Plxnb2 expression was undetectable in the EGL of En1Cre;Plxnb2fl/fl and Wnt1-Cre;Plxnb2fl/fl mice.
source: In situ hybridization with a Plxnb2 probe encompassing exons 19–23, confirmed that, unlike in Plxnb2fl/fl controls, Plxnb2 expression was undetectable in the EGL of En1Cre;Plxnb2fl/fl and Wnt1-Cre;Plxnb2fl/fl mice (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data in Figure 1F showing absence of Plxnb2 mRNA in the EGL of conditional knockouts.

claim: The EGL of En1Cre;Plxnb2fl/fl (P5) and Wnt1-Cre;Plxnb2fl/fl (P7) cerebellum was completely devoid of Plexin-B2 protein immunoreactivity.
source: In addition, the EGL of En1Cre;Plxnb2fl/fl (P5) and Wnt1-Cre;Plxnb2fl/fl (P7) cerebellum was completely devoid of Plexin-B2 protein immunoreactivity (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data in Figure 1G showing absence of Plexin-B2 protein in the EGL of conditional knockouts.

claim: A severe disorganization of the foliation and layering of the cerebellum was observed in both En1Cre;Plxnb2fl/fl and Wnt1-Cre;Plxnb2fl/fl conditional knockouts.
source: Importantly, a severe disorganization of the foliation and layering of the cerebellum was observed in both conditional knockouts (Figure 1F,G,H) which phenocopied what has been previously reported in the Plxnb2 null knockout (Figure 1B, Friedel et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Figures 1F, 1G, and 1H showing cerebellar defects in conditional knockouts.

claim: Both En1Cre;Plxnb2fl/fl and Wnt1-Cre;Plxnb2fl/fl conditional knockouts phenocopied the Plxnb2 null knockout.
source: Importantly, a severe disorganization of the foliation and layering of the cerebellum was observed in both conditional knockouts (Figure 1F,G,H) which phenocopied what has been previously reported in the Plxnb2 null knockout (Figure 1B, Friedel et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of data in Figures 1D and 1H, and by citation to Friedel et al., 2007.

claim: The mutant Purkinje cell layer showed characteristic Purkinje cell islets.
source: The mutant Purkinje cell layer (visualized using anti-Calbindin (CaBP) immunostaining, Figure 1H) showed the characteristic Purkinje cell islets, and the IGL appeared very disorganized.
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Figure 1H showing Purkinje cell islets in mutant cerebellum.

claim: The IGL appeared very disorganized in En1Cre;Plxnb2fl/fl mutants.
source: The mutant Purkinje cell layer (visualized using anti-Calbindin (CaBP) immunostaining, Figure 1H) showed the characteristic Purkinje cell islets, and the IGL appeared very disorganized.
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Figure 1H showing disorganized IGL structure in mutants.

claim: En1Cre;Plxnb2fl/fl mice displayed a more severe cerebellar phenotype than Wnt1-Cre;Plxnb2fl/fl mice.
source: We focused for the rest of the study on En1Cre;Plxnb2fl/fl knockouts as En1 has a more restricted expression than Wnt1 (which is expressed in all sensory ganglia), and En1Cre;Plxnb2fl/fl mice displayed a more severe cerebellar phenotype.
evidence: The claim is an observation from comparing the two conditional knockout lines.

claim: Midbrain defects were reported in Wnt1-Cre mice.
source: Moreover, midbrain defects were reported in Wnt1-Cre mice (Lewis et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Lewis et al., 2013.

claim: A striking delay in the formation of the cerebellar fissures was observed in En1Cre;Plxnb2fl/fl mutant mice, which was already visible at birth.
source: A striking delay in the formation of the cerebellar fissures was observed in En1Cre;Plxnb2fl/fl mutant mice, which was already visible at birth (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Figure 2A showing delayed fissure formation in mutants at P0.

claim: In normal mice, the principle cerebellar fissures start to appear from E17.5 onwards.
source: In normal mice, the principle cerebellar fissures start to appear from E17.5 onwards (Sudarov and Joyner, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Sudarov and Joyner, 2007.

claim: In control animals the six principal cerebellar fissures were clearly visible at P0, whereas the cerebellum remained smooth in the Plxnb2 mutant.
source: Whereas in control animals the six principal cerebellar fissures were clearly visible at P0, the cerebellum remained smooth in the Plxnb2 mutant (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Figure 2A showing smooth cerebellum in mutants at P0 compared to controls.

claim: Most fissures eventually emerged after P4 in En1Cre;Plxnb2fl/fl, but they were not as deep as in Plxnb2fl/fl controls.
source: Even if most fissures eventually emerged after P4 in En1Cre;Plxnb2fl/fl, they were not as deep as in Plxnb2fl/fl controls (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Figure 2A showing shallow fissures in mutants at P4.

claim: In En1Cre;Plxnb2fl/fl cKO cerebella displaced PCs were first detected at P2 but became more conspicuous from P4.
source: In En1Cre;Plxnb2fl/fl cKO cerebella displaced PCs were first detected at P2 but became more conspicuous from P4 (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Figure 2A showing ectopic Purkinje cell islets appearing at P2 and becoming more prominent at P4.

claim: 3D-light sheet fluorescence microscopy of iDISCO+ cleared brains confirmed the altered fissure formation in P4 cerebellum.
source: To better comprehend the cerebellar alterations in En1Cre;Plxnb2fl/fl cerebellum, we performed 3D-light sheet fluorescence microscopy (LSFM) of iDISCO+ cleared brains (Renier et al., 2016). Nuclear TO-PRO-3 staining confirmed the altered fissure formation in P4 cerebellum and also showed the development of additional folds of the IGL perpendicular to the main fissures (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by 3D imaging data in Figure 2B showing aberrant fissure formation.

claim: 3D imaging showed the development of additional folds of the IGL perpendicular to the main fissures in Plxnb2 mutants.
source: Nuclear TO-PRO-3 staining confirmed the altered fissure formation in P4 cerebellum and also showed the development of additional folds of the IGL perpendicular to the main fissures (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by 3D imaging data in Figure 2B showing additional folds in mutant cerebellum.

claim: Despite the aberrant folds, CGNs and Purkinje cell lamination was grossly preserved in Plxnb2 mutants.
source: Despite the aberrant folds, CGNs and Purkinje cell lamination was grossly preserved (Video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by 3D imaging data shown in Video 1.

claim: In P14 controls, cerebellar fissures were fully developed, the EGL was almost absent and IGL structure was very smooth and homogeneous.
source: In P14 controls, cerebellar fissures were fully developed, the EGL was almost absent and IGL structure was very smooth and homogeneous (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by 3D imaging data in Figure 3A showing normal P14 control cerebellum.

claim: Plxnb2 mutants at P14 showed patches of CGNs remaining at the cerebellar surface.
source: In contrast, Plxnb2 mutants showed patches of CGNs remaining at the cerebellar surface, an IGL structure with many invaginations in different orientations, and original fissures could not be defined easily (Figure 3B, Video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by 3D imaging data in Figure 3B and Video 2 showing ectopic CGN patches in P14 mutants.

claim: Plxnb2 mutants at P14 showed an IGL structure with many invaginations in different orientations.
source: In contrast, Plxnb2 mutants showed patches of CGNs remaining at the cerebellar surface, an IGL structure with many invaginations in different orientations, and original fissures could not be defined easily (Figure 3B, Video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by 3D imaging data in Figure 3B and Video 2 showing aberrant IGL structure in P14 mutants.

claim: The aberrant IGL structure and the patches of granule cells at the surface persisted in adulthood in Plxnb2 mutants.
source: The aberrant IGL structure and the patches of granule cells at the surface persisted in adulthood, well after cerebellar development was completed (Figure 3C,D, Video 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by 3D imaging data in Figures 3C and 3D and Video 3 showing persistent defects in P30 mutants.

claim: All aberrant IGL folds in the Plxnb2 mutant were lined with a monolayer of Purkinje cells.
source: All aberrant IGL folds in the Plxnb2 mutant were lined with a monolayer of Purkinje cells (Video 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by 3D imaging data in Video 4 showing Purkinje cells lining IGL folds.

claim: The Purkinje cell 'islets' observed in Plxnb2 mutant cerebellar sections correspond to stretches of Purkinje cells that line the heavily corrugated, but still continuous IGL.
source: These 3D-data convey that the Purkinje cell 'islets' observed in Plxnb2 mutant cerebellar sections actually correspond to stretches of Purkinje cells that line the heavily corrugated, but still continuous IGL.
evidence: The claim is inferred from 3D imaging data in Videos 3 and 4 showing the continuous nature of the Purkinje cell layer.

claim: A limited, but significant reduction in cerebellar volume was observed throughout cerebellar development in Plxnb2 mutants.
source: Because Plxnb2 mutant cerebella seemed to be smaller than controls on sections, we next analyzed the cerebellar volume in 3D. Indeed, a limited, but significant reduction was observed throughout cerebellar development (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A showing reduced cerebellar volume at P4 and P30.

claim: Plxnb2 mutant did not display any noticeable motor or behavioral defects.
source: Plxnb2 mutant did not display any noticeable motor or behavioral defects and their performance on an accelerating rotarod was similar to control mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by rotarod test data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B showing no significant difference between mutants and controls.

claim: The performance of Plxnb2 mutants on an accelerating rotarod was similar to control mice.
source: Plxnb2 mutant did not display any noticeable motor or behavioral defects and their performance on an accelerating rotarod was similar to control mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by rotarod test data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: In controls, EdU+ CGN precursors were usually confined to the thin outer EGL (oEGL), whereas they were more dispersed in Plxnb2 mutants.
source: In controls, whereas EdU+ CGN precursors were usually confined to the thin outer EGL (oEGL), they were more dispersed in Plxnb2 mutants (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by EdU labeling data in Figure 4A showing dispersed EdU+ cells in mutant EGL.

claim: The developing ML was much thinner in Plxnb2 mutants compared to controls.
source: In addition, the developing ML was much thinner (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data in Figure 4A showing reduced ML thickness in mutants.

claim: In control P9 cerebellum, Ki67 and Tag1 markers were segregated, whereas in Plxnb2 mutants, CGN precursors lost their confinement to the oEGL and intermingled with tangentially migrating Tag1+ CGNs in the iEGL.
source: In control P9 cerebellum, both markers were segregated (Figure 4B), whereas in Plxnb2 mutants, CGN precursors lost their confinement to the oEGL and intermingled with tangentially migrating Tag1+ CGNs in the iEGL (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by double immunostaining data in Figure 4B showing intermingling of Ki67+ and Tag1+ cells in mutants.

claim: No difference in the amount of EdU+ cells was detected for either 2 hr or 24 hr EdU administration in Plxnb2 mutants compared to controls.
source: No difference in the amount of EdU+ cells was detected for either time of EdU administration, and there was no difference in the uptake of EdU by dividing cells over time (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data in Figure 4C showing similar EdU+ cell numbers in controls and mutants.

claim: The quantification of the amount of EdU+ CGNs in the EGL that colocalized with Ki67 immunostaining did not show a difference in proliferation rate in Plxnb2-mutant brains.
source: In addition, the quantification of the amount of EdU+ CGNs in the EGL (EdU injected 2 hr before brain collection) that colocalized with Ki67 immunostaining did not show a difference in proliferation rate in Plxnb2-mutant brains (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B showing similar EdU/Ki67 colocalization in controls and mutants.

claim: A significant increase in the percentage of cells double-positive for EdU and H3P was observed in Plxnb2 mutants.
source: Interestingly, we observed a significant increase in the percentage of cells double-positive for EdU and H3P (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data in Figure 4D showing increased EdU+/H3P+ cells in mutants.

claim: The cell cycle for Plxnb2 mutant CGNs is slightly longer.
source: This implies that the cell cycle for Plxnb2 mutant CGNs is slightly longer.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the increased proportion of EdU+/H3P+ cells shown in Figure 4D.

claim: There is probably no alteration of cell cycle progression in absence of Plexin-B2 although more experiments will be required to determine if the M phase is affected.
source: Together, these results suggest that there is probably no alteration of cell cycle progression in absence of Plexin-B2 although more experiments will be required to determine if the M phase is affected.
evidence: The claim is a cautious interpretation of the data in Figure 4, acknowledging the need for further experiments.

claim: 99.6% of all targeted GFP+ cells in the cerebellum were CGNs and co-expressed Pax6 after in vivo electroporation.
source: With this method 99.6% of all targeted GFP+ cells in the cerebellum were CGNs and co-expressed Pax6 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A showing GFP/Pax6 colocalization.

claim: There was a significant reduction in the length of the processes extended by tangentially migrating CGNs in Plxnb2 mutants compared to controls.
source: By comparing the initial steps of postmitotic CGN development, we found a significant reduction in the length of the processes (and future parallel fibers) extended by tangentially migrating CGNs in Plxnb2 mutants compared to controls (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data in Figure 5D showing shorter bipolar leading and trailing processes in mutants.

claim: Cell body size and shape for proliferating and tangentially migrating CGNs was similar in both Plxnb2 mutant and control genotypes.
source: Cell body size and shape for proliferating and tangentially migrating CGNs was similar in both genotypes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B showing similar cell body width/length ratios.

claim: GFP+ CGN precursors intermingled with migrating bipolar CGNs in the EGL of Plxnb2 mutant animals.
source: As implied by the EdU and Ki67/Tag1 immunohistochemistry (Figure 4A,B), we observed that GFP+ CGN precursors intermingled with migrating bipolar CGNs in the EGL of Plxnb2 mutant animals (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 5C showing mixed distribution of multipolar and bipolar GFP+ CGNs in mutant EGL.

claim: Multipolar and bipolar CGNs in the Plxnb2 mutant were spread throughout the EGL and bipolar CGNs sometimes even resided in the ML.
source: Indeed, quantification of the location of multipolar and bipolar CGNs in the outer, inner EGL or ML, shows that multipolar and bipolar CGNs in the Plxnb2 mutant were spread throughout the EGL and that bipolar CGNs sometimes even resided in the ML (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C showing altered distribution of CGN morphologies in mutants.

claim: In Plxnb2 mutants, a fraction of the bipolar and tangentially migrating GFP+ CGNs were also labeled with EdU administered 2 hr before fixation.
source: Intriguingly, in Plxnb2 mutants, a fraction of the bipolar and tangentially migrating GFP+ CGNs, were also labeled with EdU (which only labels dividing cells), administered 2 hr before fixation.
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Figure 5C and 5E showing EdU+ bipolar GFP+ CGNs in mutants.

claim: Only a very small fraction of tangentially migrating bipolar GFP+ CGNs were EdU+ in controls.
source: By contrast, only a very small fraction of tangentially migrating bipolar GFP+ CGNs were found in controls (Figure 5C,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data in Figure 5E showing low percentage of EdU+ bipolar cells in controls.

claim: Some of the bipolar GFP+/EdU+ CGNs were indeed proliferating as shown by H3P co-expression.
source: When combining the EdU staining with H3P to mark acutely dividing cells, we could confirm that, although rare, some of the bipolar GFP+/EdU+ were indeed proliferating (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D showing GFP+/EdU+/H3P+ cells in mutants.

claim: Some bipolar GFP+ CGNs co-expressed H3P and Tag1 in Plxnb2 mutants.
source: Some bipolar GFP+ CGNs also co-expressed H3P and Tag1 (Figure 5F).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 5F showing GFP+/H3P+/Tag1+ cells in mutants.

claim: In Plxnb2 mutants, the CGN switch from proliferation to tangential migration is altered and these two phases are not spatio-temporally separated anymore.
source: This suggests that in Plxnb2 mutants, the CGN switch from proliferation to tangential migration is altered and that these two phases are not spatio-temporally separated anymore.
evidence: The claim is inferred from data in Figures 5C-F showing proliferating bipolar CGNs in mutants.

claim: There was a significant reduction in the proportion of CGNs that had initiated radial migration 48 hr after electroporation in Plxnb2 mutants.
source: To further support this hypothesis, we next analyzed GFP+ CGNs 48 hr after electroporation. Again, there was a significant reduction in the proportion of CGNs that had initiated radial migration in Plxnb2 mutants (Figure 5G).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data in Figure 5G showing fewer radial CGNs and more tangential CGNs in mutants at 2 days post-electroporation.

claim: Plxnb2-deficient CGNs might remain longer in both their proliferative and tangential phases.
source: This, together with the slight delay in M-phase (Figure 4D), suggest that Plxnb2-deficient CGNs might remain longer in both their proliferative and tangential phases.
evidence: The claim is inferred from data in Figures 4D and 5G showing delayed cell cycle and migration progression.

claim: As soon as Plxnb2 mutant CGNs started radial migration, their morphology closely resembled that of control CGNs.
source: As soon as Plxnb2 mutant CGNs started radial migration, their morphology closely resembled that of control CGNs.
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E showing similar process lengths in radially migrating CGNs.

claim: Differences in leading process length were no longer observed in radially migrating Plxnb2 mutant CGNs.
source: Differences in leading process length were no longer observed, and their ascending axons in the ML were of comparable length (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E showing similar leading process and axon lengths in radial CGNs.

claim: During radial migration, CGN cell bodies had a slightly more circular shape in Plxnb2 mutants.
source: Conversely, during radial migration, CGN cell bodies had a slightly more circular shape in Plxnb2 mutants (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E showing increased width/length ratio in mutant radial CGNs.

claim: In Plxnb2 mutants, CGNs in the IGL acquired their stereotypical CGN morphology slightly faster than in controls.
source: Moreover, in Plxnb2 mutants, CGNs in the IGL acquired their stereotypical CGN morphology with a cell body of 7–8 μm in diameter bearing 3–4 claw-shaped primary dendrites, slightly faster than in controls (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F,G).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1G showing more mutant CGNs with 4 dendrites at P20.

claim: In the IGL, CGNs might differentiate faster in Plxnb2 mutants than in controls.
source: Together, this suggests that in the IGL, CGNs might differentiate faster in Plxnb2 mutants than in controls.
evidence: The claim is inferred from data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1G showing accelerated dendrite pruning in mutants.

claim: After completion of cerebellar development, Plxnb2 mutant CGNs displayed strikingly disorganized parallel fibers.
source: After completion of cerebellar development, Plxnb2 mutant CGNs displayed strikingly disorganized parallel fibers (Figure 5H, Videos 5 and 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 5H and Videos 5 and 6 showing disorganized parallel fibers in adult mutants.

claim: Instead of being restricted to a thin sub-layer of the ML in controls, parallel fibers were more spread out in Plxnb2 mutants.
source: Instead of being restricted to a thin sub-layer of the ML in controls, parallel fibers were more spread out in Plxnb2 mutants.
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 5H showing dispersed parallel fibers in mutants.

claim: Some CGN axons were completely misprojecting deep into the cerebellar white matter in Plxnb2 mutants.
source: Some CGN axons were even completely misprojecting deep into the cerebellar white matter where they run along myelinated Purkinje cell axons and mossy fibers (Figure 5F and F-II and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 5H and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A showing CGN axons in the white matter.

claim: The ectopic CGN axons in the white matter did not get myelinated in Plxnb2 mutants.
source: The ectopic CGN axons keep some of their normal characteristics since they did not get myelinated (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B showing unmyelinated GFP+ axons in the white matter.

claim: In the IGL of Plxnb2 mutants, the labeled CGNs were more dispersed, and some formed patches at the cerebellar surface.
source: In the IGL of Plxnb2 mutants, the labeled CGNs were more dispersed, and some formed patches at the cerebellar surface (Figure 5G and HIII).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 5H showing ectopic CGN patches at the surface.

claim: According to the 'stacking model', developing parallel fibers accumulate in the ML in an inside-out time sequence, with CGNs born later extending parallel fibers above those of earlier born CGNs.
source: According to the 'stacking model', developing parallel fibers accumulate in the ML in an inside-out time sequence, with CGNs born later extending parallel fibers above those of earlier born CGNs (Espinosa and Luo, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Espinosa and Luo, 2008.

claim: The dispersion of proliferating CGNs in the Plxnb2 mutants EGL together with the presence of proliferation markers in tangentially migrating CGNs suggest that their developmental clock is perturbed.
source: The dispersion of proliferating CGNs in the Plxnb2 mutants EGL together with the presence of proliferation markers in tangentially migrating CGNS, suggest that their developmental clock is perturbed.
evidence: The claim is inferred from data in Figures 4 and 5 showing mixed proliferating and migrating CGNs in mutants.

claim: Plxnb2 mutant parallel fibers were much more scattered across the ML.
source: Accordingly, Plxnb2 mutant parallel fibers were much more scattered across the ML.
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Figure 6A showing dispersed parallel fibers in mutants.

claim: GFP+ and Tomato+ parallel fibers were clearly segregated in control mice.
source: As expected, GFP+ and Tomato+ parallel fibers were clearly segregated in control mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 6A showing segregated early and late-born parallel fibers in controls.

claim: In Plxnb2 mutants, parallel fibers lost the inside-out organization in the ML.
source: Strikingly, in Plxnb2 mutants, parallel fibers lost this inside-out organization in the ML (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 6A showing overlapping early and late-born parallel fibers in mutants.

claim: At P11, early GFP+ fibers occupied a space within the ML twice larger than in controls and largely overlap with later-born Tomato+ parallel fibers in Plxnb2 mutants.
source: At P11, early GFP+ fibers occupied a space within the ML twice larger than in controls and largely overlap with later-born Tomato+ parallel fibers, which were also more spread than in controls (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data in Figure 6A showing increased ML occupancy by GFP+ and tdTom+ fibers in mutants.

claim: In controls, nascent parallel fibers normally extend at the base of the iEGL, just above the tips of developing Purkinje dendritic arbors.
source: In controls (left panel), nascent parallel fibers normally extend at the base of the iEGL, just above the tips of developing Purkinje dendritic arbors (yellow arrowheads).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 6B showing parallel fibers at the EGL/ML border in controls.

claim: In Plxnb2 mutant, parallel fibers extend throughout the EGL and cross the Purkinje dendrites in the ML.
source: However, in Plxnb2 mutant (right panel) parallel fibers extend throughout the EGL and cross the Purkinje dendrites in the ML (yellow arrowheads indicate the tips of Purkinje dendrites).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 6B showing parallel fibers throughout the ML in mutants.

claim: In P9 Plxnb2 mutants, the young GFP+ parallel fibers ran throughout the entire ML between the Purkinje cell dendrites, which in turn appeared disorganized and more branched than controls.
source: In P9 Plxnb2 mutants, the young GFP+ parallel fibers ran throughout the entire ML between the Purkinje cell dendrites, which in turn appeared disorganized and more branched than controls.
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A showing disorganized Purkinje dendrites in mutants.

claim: In Plxnb2 mutants, Vglut1+ synapses extended to the tip of the Purkinje cell dendrites at P9.
source: Interestingly, in Plxnb2 mutants, Vglut1+ synapses extended to the tip of the Purkinje cell dendrites.
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging and quantification data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A showing increased Vglut1 density at distal dendrites in mutants.

claim: The ratio between Vglut1+ puncta at the distal ends and the proximal base of the dendritic arbor was significantly higher in Plxnb2 mutants at P9.
source: We quantified the ratio between Vglut1+ puncta (fluorescent integrated density) at the distal ends and the proximal base of the dendritic arbor, and found significantly more synapses on the distal end compared to control (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A showing increased distal/proximal Vglut1 ratio in mutants.

claim: At later stages, no difference could be observed in the distribution of CGN-Purkinje synapses between controls and Plxnb2 mutants.
source: At later stages, no difference could be observed in the distribution of CGN-Purkinje synapses (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B showing similar Vglut1 distribution at P30.

claim: In controls, nascent parallel fibers extended at the bottom of the iEGL just above the tips of Purkinje dendrites.
source: In controls, nascent parallel fibers extended at the bottom of the iEGL just above the tips of Purkinje dendrites Plxnb2 mutant brains.
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 6B showing parallel fiber position in controls.

claim: At P9, the Purkinje cells in the Plxnb2 mutant seem underdeveloped and developing parallel fibers cross the entire ML.
source: Where at P9, the Purkinje cells in the Plxnb2 mutant seem underdeveloped and developing parallel fibers cross the entire ML (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 6B showing parallel fibers throughout the ML in P9 mutants.

claim: New parallel fibers crisscrossing deep into the ML were found in P13 Plxnb2 mutant.
source: New parallel fibers crisscrossing deep into the ML were also found in P13 Plxnb2 mutant, when the ML is much larger and the Purkinje dendrites are more developed (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 6C showing parallel fibers deep in the ML in P13 mutants.

claim: CGNs exiting EGL explants follow a developmental sequence closely resembling in vivo CGNs.
source: As previously described, CGNs exiting the explants follow a developmental sequence closely resembling in vivo CGNs (Kawaji et al., 2004; Kerjan et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kawaji et al., 2004 and Kerjan et al., 2005.

claim: CGN precursors divide inside the explant or close to it in EGL explant cultures.
source: As in the oEGL, CGN precursors divide inside the explant or close to it (see below and Yacubova and Komuro, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Yacubova and Komuro, 2002 and by data in Figure 10 showing dividing cells near explants.

claim: After plating, postmitotic cells become bipolar, grow long neurites and migrate away from the explant by nuclear translocation, as during tangential migration in the iEGL.
source: After plating, postmitotic cells become bipolar, grow long neurites and migrate away from the explant by nuclear translocation, as during tangential migration in the iEGL (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 7A showing bipolar CGN migration from explants.

claim: Two to 3 days after plating, CGNs start aggregating and form satellites around the explant.
source: Two to 3 days later, CGNs start aggregating and form satellites around the explant (Figure 7A; Kawaji et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 7A and citation to Kawaji et al., 2004.

claim: The cells migrating away from the explant were CGNs as confirmed by Pax6 immunostaining.
source: Immunocytochemical analysis of young explants with Pax6, a marker for pre-and postmitotic CGNs, confirmed that the cells migrating away from the explant were CGNs (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A showing Pax6+ cells migrating from explants.

claim: Although the explant contained GFAP+ glial cells extending processes outward, their cell bodies seldom left the explant.
source: Although the explant contained GFAP+ glial cells extending processes outward, their cell bodies seldom left the explant (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B showing GFAP+ cells confined to explants.

claim: DAPI-stained nuclei from Plxnb2 mutant CGNs stayed closer to the explant compared to controls.
source: We next compared explants from P4-5 Plxnb2fl/fl or En1Cre;Plxnb2fl/fl EGL after 1 day in vitro (DIV) and noticed a difference in outward CGN migration. DAPI-stained nuclei from Plxnb2 mutant CGNs stayed closer to the explant (Figure 7B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging and quantification data in Figures 7B and 7C showing reduced migration distance in mutant explants.

claim: β-III tubulin staining revealed shorter and more fasciculated neurites in Plxnb2 mutants compared to controls.
source: Furthermore, β-III tubulin staining revealed a difference in neurite outgrowth (Figure 7B), with shorter and more fasciculated neurites in Plxnb2 mutants.
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 7B showing altered neurite morphology in mutant explants.

claim: Almost all GFP+ cells were positive for CGN markers such as Pax6 and Sema6A in EGL explant cultures.
source: Almost all GFP+ cells were positive for CGN markers such as Pax6 (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A) and Sema6A (Figure 7—figure supplement 2B), and did not resemble GFAP+ glial cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A-C showing GFP+ cells are CGNs.

claim: At DIV1 in Plxnb2 mutant explant cultures, the proportion of multipolar GFP+ CGNs was significantly increased.
source: Strikingly, at DIV1 in Plxnb2 mutant explant cultures, the proportion of multipolar GFP+ CGNs was significantly increased (65.42 ± 2.37% in mut vs. 48.88 ± 2.65% in ctl, MWU(353) p<0.0001) and the proportion of bipolar cells was decreased (Figure 7D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data in Figure 7E showing increased multipolar cells in mutant explants at DIV1.

claim: By DIV2 almost all cells – control or mutant – had a bipolar morphology in EGL explant cultures.
source: However, by DIV2 almost all cells – control or mutant – had a bipolar morphology (Figure 7D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data in Figure 7E showing most cells are bipolar at DIV2.

claim: DIV1 bipolar Plxnb2 mutant CGNs had shorter processes than control cells in EGL explant cultures.
source: Interestingly, as observed in vivo (Figure 5C), DIV1 bipolar Plxnb2 mutant CGNs had shorter processes than control cells (Figure 7D,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data in Figure 7F showing shorter leading and trailing processes in mutant bipolar CGNs.

claim: At DIV2, Plxnb2 mutant had a higher proportion of GFP+ CGNs that were not attached to the explant.
source: Finally, bipolar cells could be further subdivided into two categories: cells that connected with their trailing process to the original explant, and cells that were disconnected from the explant. Interestingly, at DIV2, Plxnb2 mutant had a higher proportion of GFP+ CGNs that were not attached to the explant (Figure 7D,G).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data in Figure 7G showing more detached bipolar cells in mutants at DIV2.

claim: Control GFP+ CGNs usually migrated away from the explant in a straight and radial direction, whereas Plxnb2 mutant GFP+ CGNs sometimes reversed direction one or even multiple times during the acquisition period.
source: Interestingly, whereas control GFP+ CGNs usually migrated away from the explant in a straight and radial direction, Plxnb2 mutant GFP+ CGNs sometimes reversed direction one or even multiple times during the acquisition period (Figure 8A, Video 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data in Figure 8A and Video 7 showing altered migration patterns in mutants.

claim: The speed of migrating bipolar CGNs was not changed in Plxnb2 mutants compared to controls.
source: Although the speed of migrating bipolar CGNs was not changed (Figure 8B), both the relative amount of distance and time going in negative direction (moving back toward the explant) were significantly increased in Plxnb2 mutant CGNs (Figure 8C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data in Figure 8B showing similar migration velocity in controls and mutants.

claim: Both the relative amount of distance and time going in negative direction were significantly increased in Plxnb2 mutant CGNs.
source: Although the speed of migrating bipolar CGNs was not changed (Figure 8B), both the relative amount of distance and time going in negative direction (moving back toward the explant) were significantly increased in Plxnb2 mutant CGNs (Figure 8C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data in Figure 8C showing increased reverse movement in mutant CGNs.

claim: In fixed DIV1 cultures, Plxnb2 mutant CGN nuclei appear closer to the explant probably because they spend more time moving in reverse direction.
source: These results probably explain why in fixed DIV1 cultures, Plxnb2 mutant CGN nuclei appear closer to the explant (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the time-lapse data in Figure 8 showing increased reverse movement in mutants.

claim: Both in vivo and in vitro data support an abnormal outgrowth of processes in Plxnb2-deficient tangentially migrating CGNs.
source: Taken together, both our in vivo and in vitro data support an abnormal outgrowth of processes in Plxnb2-deficient tangentially migrating CGNs.
evidence: The claim is a summary inference from data in Figures 5 and 7 showing shorter processes in mutant tangentially migrating CGNs.

claim: There was a much lower amount of DAPI nuclei visible around DIV1 Plxnb2 mutant explants compared to controls.
source: Although there was a much lower amount of DAPI nuclei visible around the explant (Figure 9A,B), a similar amount of EdU+ nuclei was observed (Figure 9A,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data in Figure 9B showing fewer DAPI+ cells around mutant explants.

claim: A similar amount of EdU+ nuclei was observed around DIV1 control and Plxnb2 mutant explants.
source: Although there was a much lower amount of DAPI nuclei visible around the explant (Figure 9A,B), a similar amount of EdU+ nuclei was observed (Figure 9A,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data in Figure 9C showing similar EdU+ cell numbers in controls and mutants.

claim: The explants did not show a difference in EdU+ nuclei that also stained for H3P between controls and Plxnb2 mutants.
source: In addition, the explants did not show a difference in EdU+ nuclei that also stained for H3P (Figure 9A,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data in Figure 9D showing similar EdU+/H3P+ percentages in controls and mutants.

claim: With longer application of EdU, there was no difference in the distribution of EdU between multipolar and bipolar cells at DIV1 in EGL explant cultures.
source: With longer application of EdU, there was still no difference in the distribution of EdU between multipolar and bipolar cells at DIV1 (Figure 9E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data in Figure 9F showing similar EdU+ percentages in multipolar and bipolar cells at DIV1.

claim: A larger portion of multipolar cells was positive for EdU at DIV1, suggesting that these multipolar cells were CGN precursors that escaped from the explant.
source: Nevertheless, a larger portion of multipolar cells was positive for EdU (Figure 9F), suggesting that these multipolar cells actually were CGN precursors that escaped from the explant.
evidence: The claim is inferred from quantification data in Figure 9F showing high EdU+ percentage in multipolar cells.

claim: At DIV2, many more cells with a bipolar appearance had an EdU+ nucleus in Plxnb2 mutant explants compared to controls.
source: Interestingly, at DIV2, many more cells with a bipolar appearance had an EdU+ nucleus in Plxnb2 mutant explants (Figure 9E,G).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data in Figure 9G showing increased EdU+ bipolar cells in mutants at DIV2.

claim: In mutant explants, bipolar cells are still generated long after the explants are seeded, suggesting that the in vitro proliferation of CGN precursors is differentially phased compared to controls.
source: Therefore, these data suggest that in mutant explants, bipolar cells are still generated long after the explants are seeded, suggesting that the in vitro proliferation of CGN precursors is differentially phased compared to controls.
evidence: The claim is inferred from data in Figure 9G showing EdU+ bipolar cells at DIV2 in mutants.

claim: The proportion of multipolar cells at the beginning of the time-lapse acquisition period (at DIV1) was twice as big in mutant explants compared to control.
source: As evident from the fixed cultures, the proportion of multipolar cells at the beginning of the time-lapse acquisition period (at DIV1) was twice as big in mutant explants compared to control (Figure 10—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data in Figure 10—figure supplement 1B showing increased multipolar cells in mutants at start of time-lapse.

claim: At the end of the time-lapse acquisition period (around DIV2) almost all control cells reached a bipolar state, whereas in Plxnb2 mutant explants a large portion still appeared multipolar.
source: At the end of the time-lapse acquisition period (around DIV2) almost all control cells reached a bipolar state, whereas in Plxnb2 mutant explants a large portion still appeared multipolar (Figure 10—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data in Figure 10—figure supplement 1B showing more multipolar cells in mutants at end of time-lapse.

claim: The time-lapse acquisitions of multipolar CGNs confirmed their ability to proliferate by dividing and producing two daughter cells that became bipolar.
source: The time-lapse acquisitions of multipolar CGNs confirmed their ability to proliferate. They divided and produced two daughter cells that became bipolar and henceforth commenced their tangential migration phase (Figure 10A, Video 8).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data in Figure 10A and Video 8 showing multipolar cell division.

claim: This confirms that multipolar cells are probably CGN precursors.
source: This confirms that multipolar cells are probably CGN precusors.
evidence: The claim is inferred from time-lapse data in Figure 10A showing multipolar cells dividing to produce bipolar CGNs.

claim: Before they divided, Plxnb2 mutant multipolar CGNs showed a striking increase of movement compared to controls.
